content.text: Animals and their young
By the end of this lesson I can
name and match familiar animals and their young: dog and puppy, cat and kitten, cow and calf, sheep and lamb, and hen and chick.
compare young animals with their adults, noticing that kittens look like smaller cats, while tadpoles have tails and no legs, unlike adult frogs.
Dogs and cats
A young dog is a puppy. A young cat is a kitten.

elements.alt: An adult dog beside a puppy and an adult cat beside a kitten, with all four animals fully visible and the two pairs clearly separated.
elements.name: Photo slot

slides.notes: Slide 3. Point to each animal as you say its name. Pupils echo dog, puppy, cat and kitten. Explain that young means an animal near the start of its life.

content.text: Cows and sheep
A young cow is a calf. A young sheep is a lamb.

elements.alt: An adult golden retriever and a small golden retriever puppy stand side by side, with their whole bodies visible so pupils can compare their size.
elements.name: Photo slot

slides.notes: Slide 4. Point to the adult and young in each pair. Say the names slowly and ask pupils to repeat them.

content.text: A hen and a chick
This adult bird is a hen. A young hen is a chick.

elements.alt: An adult cow stands beside a much smaller calf in a field, both shown full-length from the side with legs and hooves visible.
elements.name: Photo slot

slides.notes: Slide 5. Point to the hen and chick. Explain that chick is the name for the young bird.

content.text: Quick check
What do we call a young dog and a young cat?
What do we call a young cow and a young sheep?
What do we call a young hen?

slides.notes:
Slide 6. Read each question aloud. Give thinking time, then ask everyone to respond. Re-teach any confused pair before moving on.
Answers: 1. A puppy and a kitten. 2. A calf and a lamb. 3. A chick.

content.text: Look at the cat and kitten
Both have legs and a tail.
The kitten is smaller.
KEY IDEA
A kitten looks like a small cat.

slides.notes: Slide 7. Model comparing: first notice what is the same, then what is different. Point out the legs and tail on each animal, then compare their sizes.

content.text: A frog and its young
A young frog is a tadpole.
This tadpole has a tail and no legs.
The adult frog has legs and no tail.

elements.alt: An early-stage tadpole with a clear tail and no legs, shown whole.
elements.name: Photo slot

slides.notes: Slide 8. Explain that a tadpole looks very different from an adult frog. Trace its tail and point to the frog's legs. This photograph must show an early tadpole without legs; older tadpoles may have legs.

content.text: Quick check
How does a kitten look like an adult cat? How is it different?
How is a tadpole different from an adult frog?

slides.notes:
Slide 9. Read the questions aloud without supplying answers. Pupils work independently, using words or labelled drawings. Accept phonetic spelling. Check for the misconception that all young animals look like smaller adults.
Answers: 1. Both have legs and a tail. The kitten is smaller. 2. The tadpole has a tail and no legs. The adult frog has legs and no tail.

content.text: Exit ticket
What is a young sheep called?
Which looks like a smaller adult: a kitten or a tadpole?
An early tadpole has no legs. What does it have that an adult frog does not?

slides.notes:
Slide 10. Read aloud and collect an individual response to each question. Use the answers to identify pupils who need more practice with young-animal names or with comparing young animals and adults.
Answers: 1. A lamb. 2. A kitten looks like a smaller adult cat. 3. A tail.

objectives.text: Name and match familiar animals and their young: dog and puppy, cat and kitten, cow and calf, sheep and lamb, and hen and chick.
Compare young animals with their adults, noticing that kittens look like smaller cats, while tadpoles have tails and no legs, unlike adult frogs.
